summary: The Pandyas of Madurai were the longest-lived of the three crowned Tamil dynasties, known to Ashoka and to Roman writers for the pearls traded through their port at Korkai. Displaced by the Kalabhras, they revived under Kadungon c. 590 and fought the Pallavas for the south until the Cholas took Madurai in 910. Rising again in 1216, they overthrew the Cholas and under Jatavarman Sundara Pandya ruled from Sri Lanka to Nellore, until civil war and invasions from the Delhi Sultanate in 1311–1323 ended their empire.
details: The Pandya kingdom, centred on Madurai in the far south of the Tamil country, already existed by the 4th century BCE: the Greek envoy Megasthenes described a Pandya queen whose realm had 365 villages, each supplying the palace for one day. In the mid-3rd century BCE the rock edicts of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka named the Pandyas, with the Cholas and Cheras, among the friendly peoples beyond his frontier. The Mauryas never conquered the far south, and the Pandyas kept their independence.

The Pandyas grew rich from the pearl fisheries of their coast, traded through Korkai and Alagankulam, and from commerce with the Mediterranean. According to Nicolaus of Damascus, as reported by the geographer Strabo, an ambassador sent by a king called Pandion met the Roman emperor Augustus around 13 CE. In the 1st century CE Pliny and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea described the Pandya kingdom, and around 140 the geographer Ptolemy recorded Madurai as the royal seat of Pandion. Earlier, the Kalinga king Kharavela had boasted of taking Pandya pearls.

The Sangam poems of the early centuries CE describe Madurai as a great city and the traditional home of the Tamil literary academies. Their most famous Pandya hero is Nedunjeliyan II, who won a battle at Talaiyalanganam against the combined forces of the Chera and Chola kings and their allies. The Chera king Mantharam Cheral Irumporai was captured, though he later escaped. Dating the Sangam rulers is difficult, and the victory can be placed only roughly, in the late 2nd or early 3rd century, near the end of the early Pandya kingdom.

From around the middle of the 3rd century the Kalabhras, a dynasty whose origins remain obscure, displaced the early Pandyas and the other old Tamil royal houses. Their rule lasted until the late 6th century and is poorly documented; later Pandya inscriptions looked back on it as a time of darkness. Little is known of the Pandyas themselves for more than three centuries, although an embassy from them is recorded at the court of the Roman emperor Julian around 361. Madurai would not again be the seat of a strong Pandya king until the 590s.

Late in the 6th century the Kalabhras were overthrown. In the north the Pallava king Simhavishnu struck at them, and in the south Kadungon, who took the title Pandyadhiraja, restored Pandya rule with Madurai as his capital. The later Velvikudi inscription calls him a resplendent sun rising from the dark clouds of the Kalabhras and says he destroyed the cities of his foes. Most historians date his reign to about 590–620, though some prefer c. 560–590. The Tamil country was now divided between the Pallavas of Kanchi in the north and the Pandyas in the south.

The revived Pandyas expanded through the 7th and 8th centuries; Jatila Parantaka Nedunjadaiyan (c. 765–815) conquered the Kongu country and Venad. His son Srimara Srivallabha (c. 815–862) took the war overseas. During the reign of Sena I of Anuradhapura he launched a seaborne invasion of Sri Lanka; his forces occupied and plundered the capital, Anuradhapura, and he withdrew after making peace with the exiled king. The exact year is uncertain. At home Srimara fought the Pallavas, losing to Nandivarman III's coalition at Tellaru but winning at Kudamukku (Kumbakonam) around 859.

Sri Lanka took its revenge. King Sena II allied with a rival Pandya prince, Varaguna II, also called Maya Pandya, and sent an army to the mainland. According to the sources his forces marched on Madurai, though they failed to sack it, and placed Varaguna on the throne; some records say Srimara died of wounds soon after the fighting. Varaguna II became king around 862. The Pandya adventure in Sri Lanka had rebounded on the kingdom, and Varaguna's reign would end in a heavy defeat by a coalition from the north.

Varaguna II tried to restore Pandya power in the north of the Tamil country. Around 879 he met a coalition of the Pallava prince Aparajita, the Western Ganga king Prithvipati I and the Chola Aditya I at Thirupurambiyam, near Kumbakonam; sources date the battle between about 879 and 885. The allies won, although Prithvipati was killed and the victory was costly. The Pandyas were badly weakened and Varaguna retired. The battle is seen as a turning point: it opened the way for the Cholas, who soon overwhelmed both the Pallavas and the Pandyas.

After Thirupurambiyam the Cholas grew quickly. Aditya I annexed the Pallava kingdom, and his son Parantaka I turned south against the Pandyas. In 910 he captured Madurai, and the Pandya king Maravarman Rajasimha II fled to Sri Lanka. For about three centuries afterwards the Pandyas survived only as subordinate or rebel princes. Rajaraja I took Madurai again in the late 10th or early 11th century, Rajendra I governed the south through 'Chola Pandya' viceroys, and Kulottunga I's reign opened with a Pandya revolt that he had to put down.

By the late 12th century Chola power was fading, and the Pandyas, after a civil war of 1169–1177, recovered. Maravarman Sundara Pandya I, who became king in 1216, laid the foundation of a new Pandya supremacy. He invaded the Chola country, sacked Uraiyur and Thanjavur and drove King Kulottunga III into exile; Kulottunga later submitted and accepted Pandya overlordship. The Hoysalas of Karnataka stepped in to protect the Cholas, and at Mahendramangalam on the Kaveri a Hoysala-backed Chola army defeated the Pandyas, but the balance of power in the Tamil country had shifted south.

Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I, crowned at Chidambaram in 1251, was the greatest Pandya conqueror. He forced the Chola king Rajendra III to accept his overlordship, seized the Hoysala southern capital at Kannanur Koppam near Srirangam and confined the Hoysalas to the Mysore plateau. In 1258 his forces killed the Telugu Chola ruler Vijaya Gandagopala and took Kanchipuram, and the same year he intervened in Sri Lanka. He also defeated a Kakatiya-led army at Mudugur. By his death in 1268 Pandya power reached Nellore and Kadapa, and he gilded the roofs of the Chidambaram and Srirangam temples.

Maravarman Kulasekara I (1268–1310) completed Pandya supremacy. Around 1279 he defeated the combined forces of the Hoysala king Ramanatha and the Chola king Rajendra III, the last of his line, and afterwards the Pandyas faced no serious rival in the Tamil country. Kulasekara invaded Sri Lanka and carried the sacred Tooth Relic back to the Pandya country, and the island stayed under Pandya control until about 1308. The Venetian traveller Marco Polo, who visited in 1288 and 1293, described the kingdom and the very fine pearls found there.

When Kulasekara I died in 1310, his sons Vira Pandya and Sundara Pandya fought over the throne. The quarrel opened the way for the Delhi Sultanate, whose armies were already raiding the Deccan. In March 1311 a Khalji army under Malik Kafur marched into Pandya territory; the brothers fled, and the invaders chased them without success before returning to Delhi by late April with their plunder. The Pandyas lost south Kerala by 1312. Sundara Pandya even sought Khalji help against his brother, and another Sultanate expedition followed in 1314.

In 1323 a new Sultanate expedition led by Jauna Khan, also called Ulugh Khan and later Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq, invaded the south for his father Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq. Ulugh Khan annexed the former Pandya kingdom as the province of Ma'bar, and in the same year the Jaffna kingdom in Sri Lanka threw off Pandya influence. Around 1334 the governor Jalal ud-Din Hasan Khan declared independence and founded the Madurai Sultanate. The Pandyas survived as minor rulers based at Tenkasi until the late 16th century, but their empire was gone.
